newsitem.title: UK: Unigate joins attack on Milk Marque.
newsitem.headline: Unigate joins attack on Milk Marque.

text.p: Executives at dairy and distribution company Unigate Plc on Monday joined the attack on Milk Marque, the farmer owned group that supplies over half the milk in England and Wales, accusing it of unfairly controlling the price of milk.

Unigate chief executive Ross Buckland told reporters that his company is "heartily sick" of the process. Unigate argues that Milk Marque should not be allowed to set a lower limit on the price dairies have to pay it for milk. Buyers say the current lower limit is too high.
Milk Marque is the single largest supplier of milk in England and Wales with about a 60 percent market share.
Unigate also supports a complaint lodged by the Dairy Industry Federation to the Office of Fair Trading, which says Milk Marque should not be allowed to process, said Buckland.
"If it is allowed to process it would be totally contrary to undertakings it gave at the time it was created and it should not be permitted to proceed," he said.
Milk Marque grew out of the former monopoly body controlled by the government's Milk Marketing Board. The board, disbanded in 1994, was required by government to sell its processing arm Dairy Crest.
Dairy companies like Unigate, Northern Foods Plc and Dairy Crest Group Plc argue that if Milk Marque is allowed to sell and process milk it will have an even stronger influence on pricing.

Buyers of milk from Milk Marque say it failed to sell all its milk under contracts which began on April 1, because it had set the price too high for them to process it profitably. Milk Marque cut its milk price from April 1 to 22.1 pence per litre from about 25p in the previous year.

As a result in May Milk Marque invited tenders from both UK and offshore dairy companies to process between 900,000 and 1.8 million litres of milk a day during the summer months for a fee, leaving ownership of the product with Milk Marque.
The resulting products would then be sold into intervention, the EU's support price mechanism.
But buyers said the company failed to find anyone willing to process the surplus because of the onerous cost.
"The offer was made unfair by saying if it failed to meet the standards of intervention then the risk would lie with the processor," said Unigate finance director John Worby in an interview.
Sending its milk surplus overseas at a loss rather than selling it through the market in England and Wales at a lower price artificially inflated the price of milk offered by Milk Marque, said Worby.

Dairy companies are still seeing intense pressure on their margins from supermarket where consumers who buy four pints at once can now get a pint for 23p. Unigate saw its prices to supermarkets fall 2 percent in the last year whereas at the doorstep it managed to hold them steady.

Earlier Unigate reported a 3.4 percent increase in its pretax, pre-exceptional profits to 129.6 million pounds ($211.5 million) in the year to March 31, 1997. Compared with last year, lower commodity prices for butter and milk powder reduced operating profit by about 12 million pounds. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
